newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: BP Australia mulls retail network future.
newsitem.headline: BP Australia mulls retail network future.

text.p: Ferocious competition and the flagging profitability of its 800 Australian service stations have forced the British Petroleum Co Plc to reconsider the future of its Australian retail operations.
"That (exit) decision is going to have to come along at some stage if things don't improve in the next two to four years," BP Australia media manager Neil McMaster told Reuters.
BP Australia on Thursday posted a 38 percent fall in net profit to A$124 million in calendar 1996.

"The returns are so low at the moment - we're talking half a cent per litre - out of our retail network that we're starting with a fresh sheet of paper and saying 'what do we need to do to get back to that level of return that's acceptable to us," McMaster said.
"At the end of that exercise it may well be that people say there is nothing we can do further, but we've got to go through that exercise first."
McMaster said while sales of food and other goods helped offset losses at the fuel pump this was true only for the largest services stations situated on main roads and highways.
"The return on those sorts of products is fair but the petrol sales return is just appalling," he said.

McMaster said BP Australia's greatest barriers to improving profits, apart from competition, were national laws preventing it from owning more than five percent of service stations in its retail network.
The remainder are required to be franchised with a minimum nine year agreement, he said.
Mobil Corp, Shell Australia and Australian Petroleum Pty Ltd (Ampol) also were subject to the same restrictions but newer entrants such as Liberty and retailer Woolworths Ltd were not, McMaster said.
"We're saying remove those acts, make it more flexible for us to run our operations just as it applies to the others."
The Federal government is expected to abolish the laws towards the end of 1997 but BP would like it to happen sooner.
McMaster said the end of the siting and franchise laws would not see widespread closure of BP service stations.
"We don't want to go and boot out lots of franchisees, we just want to have more control over how we operate our network," he said.
